activities.caption: bet first — the eight minutes nobody could ignore
activities.name: okEightPredict

config.q: Kepler's circular model of Mars failed by eight arcminutes — a discrepancy almost anyone would have shrugged off. Why didn't he?
choices: He knew Tycho's data was better than that — the discrepancy forced the ellipse
He wanted fame for inventing a new shape
Eight arcminutes are visible to the naked eye
config.why: 'If I had believed that these eight minutes could be ignored, I would have patched up my hypothesis accordingly' — better data broke two millennia of circular dogma.

config.text: Earth's orbital eccentricity is a modest %%0%%, so our orbit is nearly round; perihelion sits at a(1 − e) and aphelion at a(1 %%1%% e), and they spread apart as e grows.
config.hint: e = 0 is a perfect circle; toward 1, the ellipse lengthens into a cigar.

activities.anchor: a few frantic weeks diving past the Sun
activities.caption: rebuild the comet's obedient journey
activities.name: okCometOrder

config.prompt: A comet obeys the second law perfectly. Order its journey:
items: Centuries crawling along the aphelion arc — far away, long and slow
Diving sunward, accelerating as the distance shrinks
A few frantic weeks past perihelion — short arc, fast motion
Equal areas in equal times the whole way round
config.why: Near the Sun the arc is short but fast; far away long but slow — the two effects cancel exactly (Newton: angular momentum conserved).

activities.caption: call the factor — double the distance, the year…
activities.name: okYearEstimate

config.prompt: Kepler's third law: T² = a³. Double a planet's distance from the Sun. Roughly what factor does its year grow by?
config.why: 2^1.5 ≈ 2.8 — bigger orbits take disproportionately longer, not twice as long.
config.context: The law is exact enough to say plainly: T² = a³ for anything orbiting the Sun, in years and AU.

activities.anchor: the law becomes invisible because it is everywhere true
activities.caption: file the facts — which law does each belong to?
activities.name: okLawsBuckets

items.label: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus
perihelion and aphelion spread apart as e grows
a comet crawls at aphelion and dives at perihelion
double the distance and the year grows 2.8×

config.why: Shape, speed, clock — the three laws in one breath, still the shape of every orbit in the Solar System.

config.q: Earth passes perihelion (closest to the Sun) in early January. What does that tell you about the seasons?
choices: Nothing about them — seasons come from the 23.4° axis tilt, not distance; the North has winter while nearest the Sun
January should be the hottest month everywhere
The 3% distance change is what drives the seasons
config.why: If distance caused seasons, both hemispheres would have summer together. They do not — tilted toward the Sun means higher, longer-heating sunlight; distance is a rounding error.

activities.anchor: large enough that satellites feel it and geodesists map it
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the equator's extra girth
activities.name: peBulgeEstimate

config.prompt: Equatorial diameter 12,756 km; polar diameter 12,714 km. Roughly how many km wider is Earth at the equator?
config.why: 42 km — about 0.3%, or 1 part in 300: small enough to look smooth from space, big enough that satellites feel it.
config.context: Flattening = (12,756 − 12,714) ÷ 12,756 ≈ 0.0033 — the spun-up dough of a planet turning 1,700 km/h at the equator.

activities.caption: file the layer facts — crust, mantle or core?
activities.name: peLayerBuckets

config.prompt: Four layers, mapped by listening to earthquakes. File each fact:

items.label: 5–10 km thick under oceans, 30–70 km under continents
hot, dense silicate rock down to about 2,890 km
liquid iron and nickel, 2,890–5,150 km deep
solid iron-nickel, 5,150–6,371 km — solid from pressure, not coolness
its S-wave shadow on the far side proved it molten

config.why: S waves cannot cross liquid — the shadow proved the outer core molten — and average density (5,500 vs 2,700 kg/m³ at the surface) demands iron.

activities.caption: bet first — Mars without a magnetic field
activities.name: peMarsPredict

config.q: Mars has no global magnetic field today. What follows for the planet?
choices: Its atmosphere is slowly stripped away by the solar wind
Its surface is shielded from radiation
config.why: No liquid metal core, no protective field, a very different planet — the magnetosphere is what keeps an atmosphere from being slowly stripped.

activities.caption: true or false — the molten interior
activities.name: peCoreJudge

statements.s: The Earth's core is molten rock, like lava.
statements.why: It is mostly iron and nickel — metal, not rock. Lava is melted rock, and exists only in the crust and upper mantle.

statements.s: Only the outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid under enormous pressure.
statements.why: Solid not because it is cool but because pressure crushes the metal into a fixed shape.

statements.s: S waves cross the outer core; P waves cannot.
statements.why: The reverse — S waves cannot cross liquid, so their shadow proved the outer core molten; P waves punch through.

statements.s: The swirling liquid outer core generates Earth's magnetic field.
statements.why: No liquid metal core, no field — Mars is the cautionary comparison.

activities.anchor: give or take a percent or two
activities.caption: call the magnitude — Eratosthenes' circumference
activities.name: peEratEstimate

config.prompt: Eratosthenes measured a 7.2° shadow at Alexandria, ~800 km from a well at Syene with no shadow at noon. Roughly what Earth circumference did he compute?
config.why: 7.2° is one fiftieth of a circle, so 50 × 800 = 40,000 km — against the modern pole-to-pole value of 40,008 km.
config.context: Right within a fraction of a percent, around 240 BC, with a well and a stick.

activities.caption: pair each coordinate fact with its owner
activities.name: peCoordMatch

config.prompt: Angles, not distances — match the coordinate to its behaviour:

pairs.right: angle north/south of the equator — about 111 km per degree everywhere
angle east/west of Greenwich — 111 km per degree at the equator, 56 at 60°, ~2 at 89°
the only parallel of latitude that is itself a great circle
Earth's 360° turn in 24 hours — the logic of time zones

config.why: A coordinate pair names a direction from the Earth's centre; you convert to kilometres only after deciding where you are.

activities.anchor: until the Sun is far enough below the horizon
activities.caption: bet first — why the sky is blue and the sunset red
activities.name: peSkyPredict

config.q: Why is the sky blue by day, and the sunset red?
choices: Air scatters short (blue) wavelengths far more than long (red) — scattered blue fills the sky, and at sunset the blue is scattered out en route
The ocean reflects blue upward, and red at dusk
Ozone tints the sky blue and dust tints sunsets red
config.why: Scattering strength falls as one over wavelength to the fourth power — the same physics that fills the day sky with blue paints the horizon red.
